title: Rotate the key under a table of encrypted card numbers

blocks.text: The disputes service keeps card numbers in a table, encrypted, and support finds a card's rows by a lookup value stored beside them. The key policy now says the data key changes every quarter, and the security team wants to retire the first key by the end of the year without stopping the service.

`PanVault` in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/PanVault.java` holds the keys. `rotate` makes a new data key current, `retire` destroys an old one, and `seal` already encrypts under the current key. Finish the three methods marked `TODO`:

items: `open(...)`: the card number in any record the table may hold;
`rewrap(...)`: what a background job stores in place of an old record;

blocks.text: When you're done, rows written before any number of rotations still open, every row can be moved to the current key so that old keys can be retired, and support's searches keep finding the same rows through all of it. About ten lines in total.
The tests build their keys from fixed bytes. Real keys come from a keystore or an HSM.

cases.says: a card number sealed under the current key opens again, is not stored in clear, and has a stable lookup value of its own
a record sealed before one or more rotations opens under the key its label names, not the current one
a re-encrypted record names the current key, so it still opens after the old key is retired
the lookup value of a card does not change when the data key is rotated
the lookup value depends on the secret lookup key, so a plain hash of the card number will not do

origin.section: 13.4. A Stored Card Number Names the Key That Opens It

concepts: Each encrypted card number carries the id of its key, so new records use the new key, old ones open through their label until re-encrypted, and the lookup key rotates separately.
